226: ### 6.3 Why we do **not** replicate Lone Star's $900,000-equipment defect in our own counter — and why Lone Star's residual method makes it worse than it looks
227: 
228: The question "why not allocate more to Class V and claim ordinary loss" has a clean answer for us and an uncomfortable one for Lone Star.
229: 
230: - **For us: ordinary is the worse tier, and there is no §1231 ordinary-loss/§1250 split available.** Under the library's §1245 rule, an allocation above basis produces ordinary income up to the $860,000 depreciation ceiling, and the ceiling is not reached at any price. Ordinary is 37% and capital is 20%. There is no ordinary-loss character to harvest, because equipment FMV ($650,000) is 2.7× its basis ($240,000). And §1374 will not give back a dollar of relief for extra equipment dollars, because the $230,000 equipment cap binds. So the direction of the trade is unambiguous: **every dollar into equipment costs 17 cents; every dollar out of equipment into goodwill saves 17 cents.**
231: - **For Lone Star: their own Exhibit A is internally inconsistent, and the residual method makes the $900,000 line indefensible.** Under the §1060 residual method, "FMV assets (Class V, VII) absorb FMV minus Classes I–IV, VI" (library: `irc_1060_form_8594`). Their Classes III, IV and VI total $750,000, leaving $2,350,000 to be divided between equipment (FMV $650,000) and goodwill. Goodwill is a residual by construction — so with the covenant pinned at $400,000, equipment at $900,000 is a *chosen* number $250,000 above appraisal FMV, and the residual swallows it as "goodwill of $1,450,000," which is $200,000 **below** the appraisal's goodwill-plus-trade-name FMV of $1,200,000 for 1/1/2023 plus three years of growth. Both parties must report the same allocation consistently — Exhibit A says the "allocation is binding and reported consistently on Form 8594," and the library states the same rule ("Buyer and seller report the allocation consistently," library: `irc_1060_form_8594`) — so Lone Star would be reporting $900,000 of equipment on Form 8594 to support a $900,000 depreciation basis against your appraisal. That is not an aggressive allocation, it is an audit item, and the exposure runs to *their* depreciation deductions, not just your tax.
232: - **The asymmetry to point at:** the equipment re-cut (Exhibit A's $900,000 down to $650,000) is worth **$42,500 to you today** — $250,000 moving from the 37% tier to the 20% tier. For Lone Star it is close to free: because the total price is fixed, their total step-up is $2,520,000 either way ($3,100,000 less the company's $580,000 inside aggregate basis), and a dollar of basis sheltered at 21% is worth 21 cents whichever class it sits in — $52,500 nominal on $250,000 in either column. What the higher equipment line would give them is *faster recovery* of the same shield (equipment depreciates over a short MACRS life; §197 goodwill amortizes straight over 15 years). MACRS recovery periods and PV tables are **not in the library**, so this is a labelled estimate, not a citation: the timing edge on $250,000 is about $13,100 (at 8%), $14,700 (10%) or $15,800 (12%) of present value, using standard 5-year MACRS percentages against 15-year straight §197 amortization at a 21% rate. Even on those assumptions it is barely a third of the $42,500 the misallocation costs you, cash, at closing. **Ask for the equipment line at appraisal FMV; you are asking for something that costs them a fraction of what it costs you, and it is the only defensible number anyway.**

236: ## 7. Recommendation and numbered negotiating points
237: 
238: **Recommendation: sell to Hensley at $2,850,000 stock, unless (a) Hensley will not improve the note's security or price, or (b) Lone Star will (i) re-cut the allocation as in §6.1 *and* (ii) either wait until after 12/31/2027 to close or pay a §1374 indemnity.** Run both to a signature; sign the higher *after-tax* number, not the higher price.
239: 
240: The reason Hensley wins is that the S-corp built-in-gains tax and the ordinary-income allocation together cost $237,300 + $86,700 of excess ordinary tax in the counter case (and $237,300 + $181,900 as drafted) on Lone Star's deal, while Hensley's smaller price is taxed once, at one rate. Hensley's advantage is $92,000 on the counter allocation and $187,200 as drafted — and the same two facts that hurt Lone Star are also the two that are most fixable.
241: 
242: ### Numbered negotiating points
243: 
244: 1. **Do not sign Lone Star's Exhibit A as drafted.** Tell them in writing that the equipment line must be $650,000 (Biggs & Frye 2026 FMV), not $900,000. Frame it as their exposure too: you will not sign Form 8594 reporting $900,000 of equipment, and if they depreciate a $900,000 basis built on a $650,000 appraisal, the re-cut risk is theirs. **Worth $42,500 to you; costs them only recovery timing on the same nominal shield (see §6.3).**

Offer the ancillary recital and a separately stated consulting agreement as the consideration they actually want. **Worth $68,000 ($0) or $51,000 ($100k) to you, ~$0 to them.**
246: 3. **Inventory at $140,000 carrying value, or tell them to keep it.** $1,700. Concede it early for goodwill on points 1 and 2.
247: 4. **Trade payables: get the schedule before you sign anything.** On Lone Star's deal, everything not on the schedule stays with you. Put a number on that schedule in dollars, and either (a) have Lone Star assume it all with the price held, or (b) take a price increase equal to what you keep. Also demand they pay *accrued taxes* — their §3 says "no other debt or tax." That means the entity's tax liabilities stay yours in an asset sale, and the §1374 tax is an entity tax on the LLC you still own post-closing (see point 8).
248: 5. **Inducement to sign this week: Lone Star must pay the §1374 tax.** Their deal alone triggers a $237,300 corporate-level tax that neither of you would pay on the stock deal, and it is a tax on *the LLC's* gain, which under their own §3 ("no other debt or tax") you keep. 258: ## 8. What your own estimate missed, and what is still open
259: 
260: **Your estimate: $2,480,000.** That is exactly $3,100,000 × 80% — one flat 20% rate applied to the whole purchase price, treating price as if it were all gain.
261: 
262: **The gap is $303,200** ($2,480,000 less the true as-drafted net of $2,176,800), and it decomposes exactly (all from the as-drafted Lone Star deal):
263: 
264: | Cause | Amount |
265: |---|---:|
266: | Your model's tax: 20% × $3,100,000 | $620,000 |
267: | Actual shareholder-level tax (§2.2): 37% × $1,070,000 + 20% × $1,450,000 | $685,900 |
268: | — of which: equipment §1245 recapture at 37% not 20% ($660,000 × 17 pts) | +$112,200 |
269: | — of which: non-compete at 37% not 20% ($400,000 × 17 pts) | +$68,000 |
270: | — of which: inventory margin at 37% not 20% ($10,000 × 17 pts) | +$1,700 |
271: | — offset: your model taxed $580,000 of basis recovery that is never taxed ($580,000 × 20%) | −$116,000 |
272: | Subtotal: shareholder-level understatement ($685,900 − $620,000) | $65,900 |
273: | §1374 entity-level tax — not in your model at all | +$237,300 |
274: | **Total understatement** ($65,900 + $237,300) | **$303,200** |
275: 
276: The honest framing: you applied one rate to one pool, and this transaction has **three pools at three rates** — $1,070,000 at 37%, $1,450,000 at 20%, and $237,300 at the entity level. The single item you did not know about is the entity-level tax, and it is the largest item.
277: 
278: **Two open structural questions that are not tax computations and that we could not answer from the file:**
279: 
280: - **Aggregate inside basis exceeds your outside stock basis by $160,000** ($580,000 vs. $420,000). In an asset sale, the inside basis is what shelters the gain; your outside basis is then reduced and any remaining cash distribution is taxed again. **No library authority governs S-corporation outside-basis tracking, distributions, or liquidation** (`library/INDEX.md` has no §§1367/1368), so we cannot state whether the $160,000 is lost, deferred, or converted to a loss. Our best guess, labelled as a guess: on the counter allocation with all cash distributed and the LLC liquidated, a naive reading adds about $32,000 of tax on the asset deal (basis becomes $2,702,700 against $2,862,700 of cash), which is roughly what the $160,000 of "wasted" basis costs at a blended rate. **That would widen Hensley's lead to about $124,000.** It also means the LLC must be wound up tax-efficiently, which is a second engagement.
281: - **Texas franchise tax** applies at the entity level to an S-corp in Texas. **No library authority** (`library/INDEX.md`), so it is not in any number here. Note the asymmetry: a stock sale may end the entity's Texas nexus differently than an asset sale, and Lone Star's deal expressly leaves taxes with you. Get this answered before closing either deal; it is a real, small, entity-level cost that neither LOI prices.
282: 
283: **Bottom line, in one sentence:** Hensley's $2,850,000 puts **$2,364,000** in your pocket, Lone Star's $3,100,000 puts **$2,176,800** there, and a repaired Lone Star puts $2,272,000 there — so take Hensley's money unless Lone Star pays for the tax they alone cause, in which case a delayed Lone Star closing after 12/31/2027 is the only version of their deal that beats Hensley by more than a rounding error.

memo.md:240:**Recommendation: sell to Hensley at $2,850,000 stock, unless (a) Hensley will not improve the note's security or price, or (b) Lone Star will (i) re-cut the allocation as in §6.1 *and* (ii) either wait until after 12/31/2027 to close or pay a §1374 indemnity.** Run both to a signature; sign the higher *after-tax* number, not the higher price.
memo.md:246:1. **Do not sign Lone Star's Exhibit A as drafted.** Tell them in writing that the equipment line must be $650,000 (Biggs & Frye 2026 FMV), not $900,000. Frame it as their exposure too: you will not sign Form 8594 reporting $900,000 of equipment, and if they depreciate a $900,000 basis built on a $650,000 appraisal, the re-cut risk is theirs. **Worth $42,500 to you; costs them only recovery timing on the same nominal shield (see §6.3).**
memo.md:247:2. **Non-compete at $0 or $100,000, not $400,000.** Lead with the library's rule: "A covenant not to compete is **ordinary income** to the recipient, not capital gain" and §197(d)(1)(E) denies them amortization anyway, and cite their competitor: Hensley gets the same five-year-equivalent protection for nothing. Offer the ancillary recital and a separately stated consulting agreement as the consideration they actually want. **Worth $68,000 ($0) or $51,000 ($100k) to you, ~$0 to them.**
memo.md:249:4. **Trade payables: get the schedule before you sign anything.** On Lone Star's deal, everything not on the schedule stays with you. Put a number on that schedule in dollars, and either (a) have Lone Star assume it all with the price held, or (b) take a price increase equal to what you keep. Also demand they pay *accrued taxes* — their §3 says "no other debt or tax." That means the entity's tax liabilities stay yours in an asset sale, and the §1374 tax is an entity tax on the LLC you still own post-closing (see point 8).
memo.md:250:5. **Inducement to sign this week: Lone Star must pay the §1374 tax.** Their deal alone triggers a $237,300 corporate-level tax that neither of you would pay on the stock deal, and it is a tax on *the LLC's* gain, which under their own §3 ("no other debt or tax") you keep. Name the number: **+$237,300 of price**, or a dollar-for-dollar indemnity of the §1374 tax, or move the closing to after 12/31/2027. Their alternative is to lose a $3.1M deal to a $2.85M one on tax grounds they caused. If they close after 12/31/2027, the counter-allocation net is **$2,509,300** — the best number available to you anywhere in this analysis.
memo.md:252:7. **On Hensley: get a number on the contingent liabilities, and hold the 10% cap.** Their indemnity is capped at $285,000 and the escrow is $100,000 — those are their protections, and they are fine. But "assumes all liabilities, known and unknown" needs to cover environmental and product-defect exposure on a 100-year-old cabinetry line. Ask for a **survival representation that no undisclosed liabilities exist other than on a schedule you both sign**, with that representation *not* capped at 10%.
memo.md:255:10. **Do not let the consulting agreement become your concession.** Any consulting dollars are ordinary compensation either way (library: `irc_197_and_noncompete`). If they want you for a year of training and customer introductions, price it *above* the purchase price at a market rate, separately documented, and keep it out of Exhibit A.
form_8594_counter.md:67:4. **It is Lone Star's audit exposure, not only yours.** Exhibit A itself says the "allocation is binding and reported consistently on Form 8594," and the library states the same rule: "Buyer and seller report the allocation consistently" (library: `irc_1060_form_8594`). If Lone Star signs Form 8594 reporting $900,000 of equipment and then depreciates that basis, it is claiming $250,000 of amortizable cost basis that its own appraisal contradicts. Point this out in writing. That is roughly a third of the $42,500 the line costs you in cash at closing.
form_8594_counter.md:79:- move any **consulting** obligation out of Exhibit A entirely. Lone Star's §4 bundles a five-year non-compete *and* a consulting agreement into the single $400,000 line. Consulting compensation is ordinary income whatever label the allocation puts on it (library: `irc_197_and_noncompete`), so bundling only manufactures ordinary income inside the purchase price. Any consulting arrangement should be a separate agreement, at market compensation, priced above and outside the purchase price.
form_8594_counter.md:87:Exhibit A allocates the whole $3,100,000 to Classes III–VII. The library's class list puts cash in Class I (library: `irc_1060_form_8594`), and the LOI's financing section refers to the purchase price being "adjusted for cash," so the company holds cash at closing. We cannot complete the exhibit without the number — see `QUESTIONS.md`. This is a defect in the exhibit, not a negotiating position: it must be fixed whichever allocation is agreed.
form_8594_counter.md:114:We have deliberately **not** reduced the $237,300 for any §1366(f)(2) pass-through benefit in these headline figures. The library says the built-in-gains tax "passes through to the shareholders" and can be taxed at the ordinary tier (library: `irc_1366` / `irc_1374` as indexed in `library/INDEX.md`), but it does not work the arithmetic out; we quantify that credit only as a labelled sensitivity in `memo.md` §3.3–3.4 ($47,460–$87,801) rather than bank it.

Add that neither party will file an allocation inconsistent with Exhibit A, and that a change requires both signatures.
form_8594_counter.md:131:We propose: cash at face in Class I; receivables at face; inventory at carrying value $140,000; equipment and vehicles at appraised FMV $650,000; covenant not to compete $100,000, ancillary to the sale of goodwill, with consulting separately documented and separately paid; goodwill $2,010,000. QUESTIONS.md:11:   Exhibit A allocates the entire $3,100,000 to Classes III–VII and omits Class I (cash), while the LOI's financing section says the price is "adjusted for cash" (`documents/loi_buyer_a_asset_purchase.pdf`, §§2, 8). Under §1060 cash belongs in Class I at face (library: `irc_1060_form_8594`). If the cash is *within* the price, goodwill shrinks dollar-for-dollar and reallocates; if *on top*, the adjustment is tax-free cash. The exhibit cannot be completed — or filed on Form 8594 — without the number.
QUESTIONS.md:14:   Lone Star assumes *only scheduled trade payables* and requires "no other debt or tax" (`documents/loi_buyer_a_asset_purchase.pdf`, §2); anything unscheduled stays with the company, i.e., with you, and comes out of the asset-sale net dollar-for-dollar. Hensley assumes everything, known and unknown, subject to a 12-month / $285,000 indemnity (`documents/loi_buyer_b_stock_purchase.pdf`, §3). The file contains no liability schedule at all. We deliberately excluded liabilities from every net-after-tax figure in `comparison.json`; that exclusion can only be closed with a payables schedule, a debt list, and a contingent-liability inventory (warranty, employment, environmental, open tax years). This is also where the **Texas franchise tax** exposure lives — flagged in the memo, never computed, because the library has no authority for it (the LOI statements suggest amounts may be outstanding).
QUESTIONS.md:22:6. **What are the consulting terms actually contemplated — and will you sign the covenant?**
QUESTIONS.md:23:   Lone Star's §4 bundles a five-year non-compete **and a consulting agreement** into the single $400,000 line. Is consulting a real obligation (hours, rate, duration)? Compensation for services is ordinary income whatever the allocation says (library: `irc_197_and_noncompete`), so a real consulting arrangement should sit **outside** the purchase price at market rates — that is our counter's drafting condition. Conversely, if you would not sign even a $100,000 covenant, the counter changes shape and Lone Star's value rises by $17,000 (to $2,289,000) — but a signed covenant allocated at $0 invites recharacterization (memo §6.5), so the answer is a drafting fact, not just a preference.
QUESTIONS.md:27:7. **Is either deal still open?** Lone Star's exclusivity bound you for 45 days from 3/30/2026 — through roughly 5/14/2026 — and today is 10/26/2026. Nothing in the file records an extension, termination, or counter-offer on either LOI, and both prices are now six to seven months old (`documents/loi_buyer_a_asset_purchase.pdf`, §5; memo §7). Before any of this advice is executed, confirm both buyers are live and whether either LOI has been amended since.
QUESTIONS.md:32:9. **Is Lone Star's "all cash" real?** The LOI says financed ("the purchase price is adjusted for cash") but the file contains no commitment letter or proof of funds (§8 of the LOI). A cash buyer who cannot close is worse than the unsecured note.
QUESTIONS.md:39:12. **Are there liens or secured debt on the equipment or receivables?** Nothing in the file. A UCC search matters twice: it tests Lone Star's "no other debt" closing condition, and a secured lender's lien on the assets would sit on the very equipment Exhibit A is arguing about.
QUESTIONS.md:43:14. **Which tax year do you intend to report the consulting/covenant income in, and where will you reside after closing?** No state individual income tax now (memo §1); if you move, state tax on a 2027–2028 installment stream and on the consulting income could matter. Outside the library's scope — flagging, not advising.

memo.md:29:1. **Your S-corporation is still inside the five-year built-in-gains recognition period.** The Biggs & Frye appraisal is dated 1/1/2023 and the library states the recognition period is the five years beginning with the S-election date (library: `irc_1374`). Closing in 2026 or 2027 falls inside it. An asset sale by an S-corp triggers a **corporate-level tax of $237,300** that a stock sale does not trigger at all, and you cannot reduce that tax by moving money between asset classes (Section 3).
memo.md:60:- Because the recapture ceiling is not reached, **there is no §1250 unrecaptured-gain tier to split out** — the library's own worked example is the same shape ($300k gain against $500k depreciation, all §1245 ordinary; library: `irc_1245`).
memo.md:70:**Authority:** payment for a covenant not to compete "is ordinary income to the recipient … not capital gain," because selling a business does not transfer a covenant not to compete and it "is not a 'kinds of property' transaction under §1234(b)(1). Rev. Rul. 69-643 and *H.R. Muskat Co. v. Commissioner* are the authority" (library: `irc_197_and_noncompete`). It is also §197 amortizable intangible property in the buyer's hands, and §197(d)(1)(E) "excludes from §197 a non-compete between a buyer and seller of a business" — so Lone Star cannot amortize it and Hensley will not pay for it.
memo.md:73:1. The library's rule is that a covenant "ancillary to the sale of a trade or business," given so "the seller will not compete and take away the value of the goodwill sold," is **not** separately taxable ordinary income; it is part of the goodwill sale (library: `irc_197_and_noncompete`). A five-year, five-state, no-solicit covenant delivered at closing to the buyer of substantially all your assets is the textbook ancillary covenant.
memo.md:74:2. **Hensley's own LOI takes the same position.** It gives you "a 3-year non-compete, $50,000/yr consulting (market), **no separate consideration** for non-compete" (`documents/loi_buyer_b_stock_purchase.pdf`, §5). The buyer you are using as your market benchmark prices a covenant at zero.
memo.md:92:Lone Star's LOI contemplates a separate employment/consulting arrangement. Any payments under it are ordinary compensation, not part of the sale proceeds (library: `irc_197_and_noncompete` — payments under a *separately stated* employment or consulting agreement "remain ordinary compensation"). No amount, rate, hours, or duration is in the LOI. See `QUESTIONS.md`. Any consulting dollars you can move *out* of the sale price are bad for you on the asset deal (ordinary) and equally ordinary on the stock deal, so consulting compensation should be negotiated as a cost borne by the buyer on top of price, not out of price.
memo.md:106:Brightline converted from LLC to S-corp effective 1/1/2023, and the Biggs & Frye appraisal fixed built-in gain at 1/1/2023 values (`documents/tax_history_and_conversion.md`). The recognition period is "generally the 5 years beginning with the S-election date," so it runs **1/1/2023 through 12/31/2027** (library: `irc_1374`). A sale of assets in 2026 or 2027 is inside it. The library states the operative rule without exception for a whole-company sale: "an asset that was built-in gain at conversion and is sold within the recognition period makes the S corp pay corporate tax (21%) on the built-in gain," and that tax is "passed through to shareholders under §1366(f)(2)."
memo.md:129:We have **deliberately excluded the credit from every headline number** and quantified it only as a sensitivity, worth between $47,460 and $87,801 (§3.4). Reasons: (a) the library does not state the mechanism's arithmetic — it gives the rate at which the pass-through is taxed, not how the corporate tax itself enters the shareholder's income, and no §1374(d)/§1366(f) worked example exists in the library; (b) a credit would be *worth more* on Lone Star's high-ordinary allocation than on the counter, so taking it in would understate the value of the allocation repair; and (c) the headline you should negotiate to is the one that survives if the credit does not exist. This is a judgment call, stated as such.
memo.md:143:If the asset sale closes **after 12/31/2027**, the recognition period has run and §1374 tax is $0 (library: `irc_1374`, recognition period). On the counter allocation that is worth **$237,300**, lifting the Lone Star net to **$2,509,300** and making a Lone Star asset sale the best deal on the table. The library states the five-year rule and nothing that would extend it to a sale of an operating business's receivables or inventory (the library's example is a §1231 asset), so we treat the date as a real, hard lever — subject to `QUESTIONS.md` item on the exact election date, since the period runs from the S-election date and we are inferring that date to be 1/1/2023 from the appraisal and the "effective 1/1/2023" conversion language.
memo.md:147:Hensley's LOI reserves the right to make "a §338(h)(10) or §336(e) election." **Do not consent for free.** The library states that under such an election "the target is treated as selling its assets, so the **built-in gains regime can apply**" (library: `irc_1374`). Neither LOI contains the deemed-sale allocation, so the outcome depends on an allocation Hensley's advisers will draft. Two bounding computations (assumptions stated; the §1374 tax is $237,300 in **both** because the 1/1/2023 built-in-gain caps — equipment $230,000, goodwill $900,000 — are fully absorbed once realized gain exceeds them):
memo.md:149:| Deemed allocation of Hensley's $2,850,000 | D1 — "proper" residual method: equipment capped at FMV $650,000, covenant $0 (nobody can amortize it), goodwill residual $1,850,000 | D2 — Lone Star-style dollars: AR $200,000, inventory $150,000, equipment $900,000, covenant $400,000, goodwill residual $1,200,000 |
memo.md:151:| Ordinary / capital gain | $420,000 / $1,850,000 | $1,070,000 / $1,200,000 |
memo.md:178:**Credit quality of the note (no facts to model):** Hensley's note is unsecured, no guaranty, no collateral, no subordination, no payment security, and Hensley assumes all of the company's liabilities — including trade payables — *behind* that note, i.e. the money that would otherwise pay your suppliers is the money that pays you. Hensley is a 130-employee company in three states; nothing in the file contains any financial statement, net worth, or credit data on it (assumption, flagged: we assume the note is paid; the file gives no basis to say either way). Discounting the $100,000-per-year principal stream against its $500,000 face value, an unsecured-credit haircut would be worth:
memo.md:198:- **The 45-day exclusivity is probably expired.** Lone Star's LOI is dated March 30, 2026 and binds "Exclusivity: 45 days from signing" — to roughly **May 14, 2026** (`documents/loi_buyer_a_asset_purchase.pdf`, §7). Today is October 26, 2026. **Nothing in the file records an extension or termination**, and Lone Star's LOI is otherwise "an expression of interest … not a binding agreement," and you have no fact as to whether you signed it or whether the parties have extended it (`QUESTIONS.md`). Two consequences: (a) you may be free to negotiate with Hensley now, and (b) Lone Star's price is a seven-month-old number that will not survive a re-issue without a re-cut — which is exactly why the allocation repair must be presented as part of a refreshed LOI, not as a signing comment.
memo.md:199:- **Buyer A's financing condition.** Lone Star's deal is "subject to financing" (§6). Hensley's is subject to "financing and … confirmatory due diligence … completed in 45 days" (§6). Neither is a funded deal. Neither LOI contains evidence of a commitment letter (`QUESTIONS.md`).
memo.md:225:2. **You can price the covenant and still win the ancillary argument, if the drafting is right.** The library's own cure is drafting, not denial: state that the covenant is ancillary to the sale of the business, and put any consulting obligation in a **separately stated** employment/consulting agreement at compensation you can defend. A modest, non-zero, defensible covenant number ($100,000 = 3.2% of price) is far easier to defend than a $400,000 number, and a lot easier than $0 with a signed covenant.
memo.md:226:3. **The ladder lets Lone Star choose, which is how you get the equipment fix accepted.** Offer: covenant at **$0** (their preference) *only if* equipment goes to $650,000 FMV and the covenant recital states it is ancillary to the sale of goodwill; covenant at **$100,000** as our draft; covenant at $400,000 only with equipment at $650,000, which costs them nothing and us $51,000 and which we will not recommend. Every rung gives them something.

# 2026 individual rates used in this engagement

*Citation:* IRC §1(h), §1(j); §1411  
*Status in this library:* in force

For this engagement use: ordinary income marginal rate **37%**; long-term capital gain **20%**; the 3.8% net investment income tax does **not** apply to gain from an active trade or business in which the taxpayer materially participates. Texas has no individual income tax.
=== irc_1060_form_8594.md ===
# IRC §1060 and Form 8594 — residual method

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §1060; Treas. Reg. §1.1060-1; Form 8594 Instructions  
*Status in this library:* in force

In an applicable asset acquisition, consideration is allocated under the residual method among seven classes in order: I cash; II actively traded personal property; III mark-to-market assets and receivables; IV inventory; V all other assets (equipment, real property); VI section 197 intangibles other than goodwill (including covenants not to compete); VII goodwill and going concern value. Each class is allocated up to fair market value before moving to the next. **Buyer and seller must each file Form 8594 and report consistently** with any written allocation agreement.
=== irc_1245.md ===
# IRC §1245 — gain from dispositions of certain depreciable property

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §1245(a)(1)  
*Status in this library:* in force

If section 1245 property is disposed of, the amount by which the lower of (A) the recomputed basis of the property, or (B) the amount realized, exceeds the adjusted basis of such property **shall be treated as ordinary income**. (Recomputed basis = adjusted basis plus depreciation allowed or allowable.) Such gain is recognized notwithstanding any other provision of this subtitle.
=== irc_1374.md ===
# IRC §1374 — tax imposed on certain built-in gains

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §1374(a), (b), (d)(7)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) If for any taxable year beginning in the **recognition period** an S corporation has a net recognized built-in gain, there is imposed a tax (computed under subsection (b)) on the income of such corporation for such taxable year. (b)(1) The tax is the highest corporate rate (**21%**) on the net recognized built-in gain. (d)(7) The recognition period is the **5-year period beginning with the first day of the first taxable year for which the corporation was an S corporation**. Recognized built-in gain on an asset is limited to the asset's built-in gain at the start of the recognition period. The tax paid is treated as a loss sustained by the S corporation (§1366(f)(2)).
=== irc_197_and_noncompete.md ===
# IRC §197 and covenants not to compete

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §197(d)(1)(E); Rev. Rul. 69-643; *Muskat v. United States*, 554 F.3d 183 (1st Cir. 2009)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A covenant not to compete entered into in connection with the acquisition of a trade or business is a section 197 intangible amortizable by the buyer over 15 years. **To the seller, payments for a covenant not to compete are ordinary income** (compensation for refraining from competing), not capital gain. Allocation between a covenant and goodwill must reflect economic reality; the parties' written allocation is binding on them (§1060(a); *Danielson* rule) absent strong proof, and the IRS may challenge it.
=== irc_453_installment.md ===
# IRC §453 — installment method

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §453(a), (b), (i)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Income from an installment sale is taken into account under the installment method (gain recognized proportionately as payments are received), **except** that recapture income under §1245 is recognized in the year of sale regardless of payments (§453(i)), and the method is not available for inventory or for sales of depreciable property to related persons.
=== stock_vs_asset_overview.md ===
# Stock vs asset sale — tax and liability overview

*Citation:* Practitioner summary  
*Status in this library:* in force

Stock (membership-interest) sale: seller recognizes capital gain on the difference between price and stock basis; buyer takes carryover basis in assets (no step-up unless a §338(h)(10)/§336(e) election, which converts the deal to a deemed asset sale with asset-sale consequences to the seller); buyer inherits all liabilities. Asset sale: gain computed asset by asset under the allocation; recapture and covenant payments are ordinary; buyer gets a basis step-up; S corporations within the §1374 recognition period owe entity-level built-in gains tax. Price differences between the two structures typically reflect the buyer's step-up value and assumed liabilities.

## 1. Bottom line

| | Lone Star as drafted | Lone Star with our counter allocation | Hensley stock sale |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Price / consideration | $3,100,000 | $3,100,000 | $2,850,000 |
| Ordinary income (37%) | $1,070,000 | $510,000 | $0 |
| Long-term capital gain (20%) | $1,450,000 | $2,010,000 | $2,430,000 |
| Shareholder-level tax | $685,900 | $590,700 | $486,000 |
| Entity-level §1374 tax (21%) | $237,300 | $237,300 | $0 |
| **Total tax** | **$923,200** | **$828,000** | **$486,000** |
| **Net after tax** | **$2,176,800** | **$2,272,000** | **$2,364,000** |

(Hensley's figure excludes the note's interest; the interest adds $56,700 after tax — Section 7.2. All figures are nominal and undiscounted; definitions in Section 1.2.)

**Hensley pays $250,000 less and leaves you $187,200 more than Lone Star as drafted — even before its note pays you interest.** Lone Star's own allocation is what makes its bigger price smaller: the $400,000 you would book to the non-compete is ordinary at 37%, and its $900,000 equipment line exceeds documented fair value, so all $660,000 of equipment gain is §1245 recapture at 37%. Fixing the allocation at the same $3,100,000 is worth $95,200 to you. Even then, Hensley still leads the repaired Lone Star deal by $92,000 — Hensley's structure avoids both the ordinary-income trap and the $237,300 entity-level tax outright.

### 1.1 The three things that drive the entire result

1. **Your S corporation is still inside the five-year built-in-gains recognition period.** The S election is effective January 1, 2023 (CPA memo), and the library states the recognition period is the "5-year period beginning with the first day of the first taxable year for which the corporation was an S corporation" (library: `irc_1374`). A 2026 closing is inside it. An asset sale by an S corporation in the period triggers a **corporate-level tax of $237,300** that a stock sale does not trigger at all — and you cannot reduce it by moving money between asset classes, because the law limits recognized built-in gain to each asset's built-in gain at the start of the period (Section 4).
2. **Lone Star's allocation manufactures ordinary income.** Under the library, covenant payments to a seller are ordinary income and recapture is ordinary (library: `irc_197_and_noncompete`, `irc_1245`, `stock_vs_asset_overview`). As drafted, $1,070,000 — 35% of the price — is taxed at 37% instead of 20%.
3. **Almost none of the price is sheltered by basis.** Your stock basis is $420,000 (CPA memo, as of 12/31/2025) and the company's aggregate inside asset basis is $580,000 (register equipment $240,000 + CPA-memo inventory $140,000 + receivables $200,000 if the receivables carry full basis — Section 3.1), against prices of $2.85M and $3.1M. And inside basis exceeds your outside basis by $160,000, which an asset sale largely wastes (Section 8.4).

### 1.2 What "net after tax" means here (and what it does not)

- Headline net = consideration minus (shareholder-level tax + entity-level §1374 tax), **nominal and undiscounted**.
- Hensley's note interest ($90,000 total, $56,700 after tax at 37%) is a return *on* the note, not on the deal; it is reported separately, not in the headline. Including it, Hensley's nominal net is $2,420,700.

- Your stock basis is assumed unchanged from 12/31/2025 to the closing date; the file gives no 2026 activity (QUESTIONS.md).

### 1.3 Recommendation (detail in Section 10)

Pursue Hensley at $2,850,000 — but use a corrected Lone Star allocation (Section 6) both to force Lone Star to pay for its defective exhibit and to make Hensley compete. Do not sign the Lone Star LOI as drafted. Do not give Hensley §338(h)(10)/§336(e) consent for free — a deemed asset sale at their price costs you $276,700–$387,200 (Section 7.5). If it were held to apply, add 3.8% to the capital-gain rate — roughly $92,340 on the Hensley gain; it is in QUESTIONS.md.

Gain = amount realized minus adjusted basis; basis recovery is not taxed but reduces what is. That is the standard method; the library does not spell the formula out, so it is labelled as such wherever it does work (Sections 3, 8).

2. **Class I is missing.** Exhibit A totals $3,100,000 across Classes III–VII only. There is no Class I line for cash in the company at closing. 3. Also note: Exhibit A's Class VII goodwill is $1,450,000, while the 2023 appraisal valued goodwill/trade name at $900,000. ---

## 4. The §1374 built-in gains tax: $237,300 in every asset-sale scenario, and why you cannot allocate your way out of it

### 4.1 You are inside the recognition period

Library (`irc_1374`): "(a) If for any taxable year beginning in the **recognition period** an S corporation has a net recognized built-in gain, there is imposed a tax… (b)(1) The tax is the highest corporate rate (**21%**) on the net recognized built-in gain. (d)(7) The recognition period is the **5-year period beginning with the first day of the first taxable year for which the corporation was an S corporation.**"

The CPA memo: "Elected S corporation status effective January 1, 2023 (Form 2553 accepted)." Recognition period = **January 1, 2023 through December 31, 2027**. Any 2026 or 2027 closing is inside it.

### 4.2 The computation, capped at the conversion values

The library adds the ceiling that decides everything: "Recognized built-in gain on an asset is limited to the asset's built-in gain at the start of the recognition period" (`irc_1374`). The CPA's conversion appraisal fixed exactly that at 1/1/2023:

| Asset | FMV at 1/1/2023 | Adjusted basis at 1/1/2023 | Built-in gain (cap) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Goodwill / trade name | $900,000 | $0 | $900,000 |
| Equipment & vehicles | $610,000 | $380,000 | $230,000 |
| Other | — | — | $0 |

(The appraisal was obtained by the prior CPA; the file does not name the appraiser. The register's 2026 equipment FMV of $650,000 exceeds the 2023 appraisal's $610,000 — irrelevant: the cap is frozen at 1/1/2023 values.)

Under **every** allocation tested in this memo, actual recognized gain in the capped assets exceeds their caps — equipment gain is $660,000 (drafted) or $410,000 (counter), both above $230,000; goodwill gain is $1,450,000 (drafted) or $2,010,000 (counter), both above $900,000. So:

**Net recognized built-in gain = $230,000 + $900,000 = $1,130,000. Entity tax = $1,130,000 × 21% = $237,300.**

(The library's §1374 text imposes the tax on "net recognized built-in gain" without spelling out the netting mechanics; taking the two capped asset amounts at face value is the straightforward reading and is labelled as such. Note also the C-corporation history — 2012 to 2022, elected "at the lender's request" (CPA memo). The library's period runs from the first S year with no C-carryover concept, so nothing is modeled from those years; QUESTIONS.md asks whether any pre-2023 items could affect the computation.)

### 4.3 Re-allocating price does **not** reduce this tax

The cap is per-asset at the start of the period, not a percentage of price. Shifting dollars between Classes IV, V, VI and VII changes your **shareholder-level** character (Section 6) but leaves the entity's $237,300 untouched — as drafted, countered, at covenant $0, or at any price from $2.85M to $3.4M tested here, both caps are fully absorbed. Corollary for negotiation: at the margin, extra price lands in the goodwill residual at 20% with **no additional §1374**, so every incremental dollar of Lone Star price nets you 80 cents.

### 4.4 The §1366(f)(2) credit — a genuine open question, kept out of the headline

The library's §1374 ends: "The tax paid is treated as a loss sustained by the S corporation (§1366(f)(2))." Read at face value, that $237,300 loss passes through to you and offsets your own gain, saving somewhere between $47,460 (if it shelters capital gain at 20%) and $87,801 (if ordinary at 37%). The library contains no §1366 text — no character, ordering, or timing rules — so we cannot verify how (or in what year) it actually applies to a one-year entity. **The headline treats the §1374 tax as a straight cash cost and this credit as an unverified sensitivity.** It does not change the ranking: the stock sale avoids the entity tax entirely, so the credit is worth something only on the Lone Star route.

### 4.5 The one clean escape: wait out the period — and its price

The recognition period ends 12/31/2027. A closing in 2028 pays **$0** §1374 tax: under the counter allocation your net would be $2,272,000 + $237,300 = **$2,509,300** — more than Hensley by $145,300 even before interest. That prices the lever at $237,300. It is commercially unrealistic with these buyers (Lone Star's LOI is cash-at-closing now; Hensley's note already starts in year 1), but it is worth knowing what you are conceding, and it is the only legally clean route around §1374 the file supports.

---

## 5. Lone Star as drafted: $2,176,800 net on a $3.1M price

Exhibit A (LOI A): III receivables $200,000 / IV inventory $150,000 / V equipment & vehicles $900,000 / VI non-compete $400,000 / VII goodwill $1,450,000 = $3,100,000, "to be reported consistently by both parties on IRS Form 8594" (LOI A §3; the library: "**Buyer and seller must each file Form 8594 and report consistently** with any written allocation agreement").

| Component | Allocated | Basis | Gain | Character | Tax |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| III Receivables | $200,000 | $200,000 (assumed) | $0 | — | $0 |
| IV Inventory | $150,000 | $140,000 | $10,000 | Ordinary | $3,700 |
| V Equipment & vehicles | $900,000 | $240,000 | $660,000 | Ordinary (§1245, Section 3.3) | $244,200 |
| VI Non-compete | $400,000 | $0 | $400,000 | Ordinary (§197/Rev. Rul. 69-643) | $148,000 |
| VII Goodwill (residual) | $1,450,000 | $0 | $1,450,000 | LTCG | $290,000 |
| **Shareholder subtotal** | | | $2,520,000 | $1,070,000 ord / $1,450,000 cap | **$685,900** |
| Entity §1374 (Section 4.2) | | | | | **$237,300** |
| **Total tax** | | | | | **$923,200** |
| **Net** | | | | | **$2,176,800** |

Arithmetic: 37% × $1,070,000 = $395,900; 20% × $1,450,000 = $290,000; $395,900 + $290,000 = $685,900; + $237,300 = $923,200; $3,100,000 − $923,200 = $2,176,800. Effective rate on price: 29.78%.

Note what you are also agreeing to: LOI A §4 puts **you** personally in a 5-year covenant *and* consulting obligation for a $400,000 allocation that is taxed at your worst rate; LOI A §1 makes you deliver the receivables (Section 3.1 sensitivity); and Exhibit A as filed would be a written allocation "binding on them" (library: `irc_197_and_noncompete`) against the IRS for both parties. LOI A §5 makes the LOI "Non-binding except confidentiality and exclusivity (45 days)" — non-binding terms, but the exclusivity may already bind you alone (Section 10.1).

---

## 6. The counter allocation: +$95,200 at the same price, and what each line is worth

### 6.1 The counter (full justification and filing mechanics in `form_8594_counter.md`)

| Class | Line | Exhibit A | **Counter** | Basis | Gain | Character |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| III | Receivables | $200,000 | $200,000 | $200,000 (assumed) | $0 | — |
| IV | Inventory | $150,000 | $140,000 | $140,000 | $0 | — |
| V | Equipment & vehicles | $900,000 | $650,000 | $240,000 | $410,000 | Ordinary in full |
| VI | Non-compete | $400,000 | $100,000 | $0 | $100,000 | Ordinary |
| VII | Goodwill (residual) | $1,450,000 | $2,010,000 | $0 | $2,010,000 | LTCG |
| | **Total** | $3,100,000 | **$3,100,000** | | $2,520,000 | $510,000 ord / $2,010,000 cap |

Tax: 37% × $510,000 = $188,700; 20% × $2,010,000 = $402,000; shareholder $590,700; entity §1374 $237,300 (unchanged — Section 4.3); total $828,000; **net $2,272,000**. **Gain: $2,272,000 − $2,176,800 = $95,200.**

The arithmetic identity: every dollar moved from Class IV/V/VI into the Class VII residual moves from 37% to 20% — **17 points** — and triggers no extra §1374 because both caps are already fully absorbed:

| Fix | Dollars | Value (17%) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Equipment $900,000 → $650,000 (your own register's FMV) | $250,000 | $42,500 |
| Covenant $400,000 → $100,000 (economic-reality rule, Section 3.4) | $300,000 | $51,000 |
| Inventory $150,000 → $140,000 (CPA carrying value) | $10,000 | $1,700 |
| **Total** | | **$95,200** |

### 6.2 Why covenant $100,000 and not $0

$0 is the economically honest number against the appraisal and the Hensley datapoint, and it is worth the most: covenant at $0 yields ordinary $410,000, capital $2,110,000, tax $573,700 + $237,300 = $811,000, **net $2,289,000** (+$112,200 vs. drafted). But a signed exhibit that pays you **nothing** for a 5-year covenant you refuse to walk away from invites exactly the re-characterization the library warns about: the written allocation is binding absent "strong proof" and the IRS may challenge an allocation that does not reflect economic reality (`irc_197_and_noncompete`). A deal with a 5-year covenant and literally zero allocated to it is the classic fact pattern for the IRS to pull dollars out of goodwill into ordinary income — with interest — on an allocation you signed. **Counter at $100,000 (judgement, labelled), concede toward $0 only in exchange for price, and never below a token real number.** Tier map (same equipment and inventory lines throughout):

| Covenant | Ordinary | Capital | Total tax | Net |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $0 | $410,000 | $2,110,000 | $811,000 | $2,289,000 |
| $100,000 | $510,000 | $2,010,000 | $828,000 | $2,272,000 |
| $400,000 (drafted) | $1,070,000 | $1,450,000 | $923,200 | $2,176,800 |

Each $100,000 of covenant costs you $17,000. That is the price of the risk shield — say so out loud when you negotiate it.

### 6.3 What Lone Star's concessions are actually worth to them (know your trading currency)

# 2026 individual rates used in this engagement

*Citation:* IRC §1(h), §1(j); §1411  
*Status in this library:* in force

For this engagement use: ordinary income marginal rate **37%**; long-term capital gain **20%**; the 3.8% net investment income tax does **not** apply to gain from an active trade or business in which the taxpayer materially participates. Texas has no individual income tax.
===== irc_1060_form_8594.md =====
# IRC §1060 and Form 8594 — residual method

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §1060; Treas. Reg. §1.1060-1; Form 8594 Instructions  
*Status in this library:* in force

In an applicable asset acquisition, consideration is allocated under the residual method among seven classes in order: I cash; II actively traded personal property; III mark-to-market assets and receivables; IV inventory; V all other assets (equipment, real property); VI section 197 intangibles other than goodwill (including covenants not to compete); VII goodwill and going concern value. Each class is allocated up to fair market value before moving to the next. **Buyer and seller must each file Form 8594 and report consistently** with any written allocation agreement.
===== irc_1245.md =====
# IRC §1245 — gain from dispositions of certain depreciable property

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §1245(a)(1)  
*Status in this library:* in force

If section 1245 property is disposed of, the amount by which the lower of (A) the recomputed basis of the property, or (B) the amount realized, exceeds the adjusted basis of such property **shall be treated as ordinary income**. (Recomputed basis = adjusted basis plus depreciation allowed or allowable.) Such gain is recognized notwithstanding any other provision of this subtitle.
===== irc_1374.md =====
# IRC §1374 — tax imposed on certain built-in gains

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §1374(a), (b), (d)(7)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) If for any taxable year beginning in the **recognition period** an S corporation has a net recognized built-in gain, there is imposed a tax (computed under subsection (b)) on the income of such corporation for such taxable year. (b)(1) The tax is the highest corporate rate (**21%**) on the net recognized built-in gain. (d)(7) The recognition period is the **5-year period beginning with the first day of the first taxable year for which the corporation was an S corporation**. Recognized built-in gain on an asset is limited to the asset's built-in gain at the start of the recognition period. The tax paid is treated as a loss sustained by the S corporation (§1366(f)(2)).
===== irc_197_and_noncompete.md =====
# IRC §197 and covenants not to compete

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §197(d)(1)(E); Rev. Rul. 69-643; *Muskat v. United States*, 554 F.3d 183 (1st Cir. 2009)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A covenant not to compete entered into in connection with the acquisition of a trade or business is a section 197 intangible amortizable by the buyer over 15 years. **To the seller, payments for a covenant not to compete are ordinary income** (compensation for refraining from competing), not capital gain. Allocation between a covenant and goodwill must reflect economic reality; the parties' written allocation is binding on them (§1060(a); *Danielson* rule) absent strong proof, and the IRS may challenge it.
===== irc_453_installment.md =====
# IRC §453 — installment method

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §453(a), (b), (i)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Income from an installment sale is taken into account under the installment method (gain recognized proportionately as payments are received), **except** that recapture income under §1245 is recognized in the year of sale regardless of payments (§453(i)), and the method is not available for inventory or for sales of depreciable property to related persons.
===== stock_vs_asset_overview.md =====
# Stock vs asset sale — tax and liability overview

*Citation:* Practitioner summary  
*Status in this library:* in force

Stock (membership-interest) sale: seller recognizes capital gain on the difference between price and stock basis; buyer takes carryover basis in assets (no step-up unless a §338(h)(10)/§336(e) election, which converts the deal to a deemed asset sale with asset-sale consequences to the seller); buyer inherits all liabilities. Asset sale: gain computed asset by asset under the allocation; recapture and covenant payments are ordinary; buyer gets a basis step-up; S corporations within the §1374 recognition period owe entity-level built-in gains tax. Price differences between the two structures typically reflect the buyer's step-up value and assumed liabilities.

===== irc_1374.md =====
# IRC §1374 — tax imposed on certain built-in gains

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §1374(a), (b), (d)(7)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) If for any taxable year beginning in the **recognition period** an S corporation has a net recognized built-in gain, there is imposed a tax (computed under subsection (b)) on the income of such corporation for such taxable year. (b)(1) The tax is the highest corporate rate (**21%**) on the net recognized built-in gain. (d)(7) The recognition period is the **5-year period beginning with the first day of the first taxable year for which the corporation was an S corporation**. Recognized built-in gain on an asset is limited to the asset's built-in gain at the start of the recognition period. The tax paid is treated as a loss sustained by the S corporation (§1366(f)(2)).
===== irc_197_and_noncompete.md =====
# IRC §197 and covenants not to compete

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §197(d)(1)(E); Rev. Rul. 69-643; *Muskat v. United States*, 554 F.3d 183 (1st Cir. 2009)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A covenant not to compete entered into in connection with the acquisition of a trade or business is a section 197 intangible amortizable by the buyer over 15 years. **To the seller, payments for a covenant not to compete are ordinary income** (compensation for refraining from competing), not capital gain. Allocation between a covenant and goodwill must reflect economic reality; the parties' written allocation is binding on them (§1060(a); *Danielson* rule) absent strong proof, and the IRS may challenge it.
===== irc_453_installment.md =====
# IRC §453 — installment method

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §453(a), (b), (i)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Income from an installment sale is taken into account under the installment method (gain recognized proportionately as payments are received), **except** that recapture income under §1245 is recognized in the year of sale regardless of payments (§453(i)), and the method is not available for inventory or for sales of depreciable property to related persons.
===== stock_vs_asset_overview.md =====
# Stock vs asset sale — tax and liability overview

*Citation:* Practitioner summary  
*Status in this library:* in force

Stock (membership-interest) sale: seller recognizes capital gain on the difference between price and stock basis; buyer takes carryover basis in assets (no step-up unless a §338(h)(10)/§336(e) election, which converts the deal to a deemed asset sale with asset-sale consequences to the seller); buyer inherits all liabilities. Asset sale: gain computed asset by asset under the allocation; recapture and covenant payments are ordinary; buyer gets a basis step-up; S corporations within the §1374 recognition period owe entity-level built-in gains tax. Price differences between the two structures typically reflect the buyer's step-up value and assumed liabilities.

34: ### 1.2 What "net after tax" means here (and what it does not)

41: ### 1.3 Recommendation (detail in Section 10)

109: ## 4. The §1374 built-in gains tax: $237,300 in every asset-sale scenario, and why you cannot allocate your way out of it
110: 
111: ### 4.1 You are inside the recognition period
112: 
113: Library (`irc_1374`): "(a) If for any taxable year beginning in the **recognition period** an S corporation has a net recognized built-in gain, there is imposed a tax… (b)(1) The tax is the highest corporate rate (**21%**) on the net recognized built-in gain. (d)(7) The recognition period is the **5-year period beginning with the first day of the first taxable year for which the corporation was an S corporation.**"
114: 
115: The CPA memo: "Elected S corporation status effective January 1, 2023 (Form 2553 accepted)." Recognition period = **January 1, 2023 through December 31, 2027**. Any 2026 or 2027 closing is inside it.
116: 
117: ### 4.2 The computation, capped at the conversion values
118: 
119: The library adds the ceiling that decides everything: "Recognized built-in gain on an asset is limited to the asset's built-in gain at the start of the recognition period" (`irc_1374`). The CPA's conversion appraisal fixed exactly that at 1/1/2023:
120: 
121: | Asset | FMV at 1/1/2023 | Adjusted basis at 1/1/2023 | Built-in gain (cap) |
122: |---|---:|---:|---:|
123: | Goodwill / trade name | $900,000 | $0 | $900,000 |
124: | Equipment & vehicles | $610,000 | $380,000 | $230,000 |
125: | Other | — | — | $0 |
126: 
127: (The appraisal was obtained by the prior CPA; the file does not name the appraiser. The register's 2026 equipment FMV of $650,000 exceeds the 2023 appraisal's $610,000 — irrelevant: the cap is frozen at 1/1/2023 values.)
128: 
129: Under **every** allocation tested in this memo, actual recognized gain in the capped assets exceeds their caps — equipment gain is $660,000 (drafted) or $410,000 (counter), both above $230,000; goodwill gain is $1,450,000 (drafted) or $2,010,000 (counter), both above $900,000. So:
130: 
131: **Net recognized built-in gain = $230,000 + $900,000 = $1,130,000. Entity tax = $1,130,000 × 21% = $237,300.**
132: 
133: (The library's §1374 text imposes the tax on "net recognized built-in gain" without spelling out the netting mechanics; taking the two capped asset amounts at face value is the straightforward reading and is labelled as such. Note also the C-corporation history — 2012 to 2022, elected "at the lender's request" (CPA memo). The library's period runs from the first S year with no C-carryover concept, so nothing is modeled from those years; QUESTIONS.md asks whether any pre-2023 items could affect the computation.)
134: 
135: ### 4.3 Re-allocating price does **not** reduce this tax
136: 
137: The cap is per-asset at the start of the period, not a percentage of price. Shifting dollars between Classes IV, V, VI and VII changes your **shareholder-level** character (Section 6) but leaves the entity's $237,300 untouched — as drafted, countered, at covenant $0, or at any price from $2.85M to $3.4M tested here, both caps are fully absorbed. Corollary for negotiation: at the margin, extra price lands in the goodwill residual at 20% with **no additional §1374**, so every incremental dollar of Lone Star price nets you 80 cents.
138: 
139: ### 4.4 The §1366(f)(2) credit — a genuine open question, kept out of the headline
140: 
141: The library's §1374 ends: "The tax paid is treated as a loss sustained by the S corporation (§1366(f)(2))." Read at face value, that $237,300 loss passes through to you and offsets your own gain, saving somewhere between $47,460 (if it shelters capital gain at 20%) and $87,801 (if ordinary at 37%). The library contains no §1366 text — no character, ordering, or timing rules — so we cannot verify how (or in what year) it actually applies to a one-year entity. **The headline treats the §1374 tax as a straight cash cost and this credit as an unverified sensitivity.** It does not change the ranking: the stock sale avoids the entity tax entirely, so the credit is worth something only on the Lone Star route.
142: 
143: ### 4.5 The one clean escape: wait out the period — and its price
144: 
145: The recognition period ends 12/31/2027. A closing in 2028 pays **$0** §1374 tax: under the counter allocation your net would be $2,272,000 + $237,300 = **$2,509,300** — more than Hensley by $145,300 even before interest. That prices the lever at $237,300. It is commercially unrealistic with these buyers (Lone Star's LOI is cash-at-closing now; Hensley's note already starts in year 1), but it is worth knowing what you are conceding, and it is the only legally clean route around §1374 the file supports.

149: ## 5. Lone Star as drafted: $2,176,800 net on a $3.1M price
150: 
151: Exhibit A (LOI A): III receivables $200,000 / IV inventory $150,000 / V equipment & vehicles $900,000 / VI non-compete $400,000 / VII goodwill $1,450,000 = $3,100,000, "to be reported consistently by both parties on IRS Form 8594" (LOI A §3; the library: "**Buyer and seller must each file Form 8594 and report consistently** with any written allocation agreement").

154: |---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
155: | III Receivables | $200,000 | $200,000 (assumed) | $0 | — | $0 |
156: | IV Inventory | $150,000 | $140,000 | $10,000 | Ordinary | $3,700 |
157: | V Equipment & vehicles | $900,000 | $240,000 | $660,000 | Ordinary (§1245, Section 3.3) | $244,200 |
158: | VI Non-compete | $400,000 | $0 | $400,000 | Ordinary (§197/Rev. Rul. 69-643) | $148,000 |

167: Note what you are also agreeing to: LOI A §4 puts **you** personally in a 5-year covenant *and* consulting obligation for a $400,000 allocation that is taxed at your worst rate; LOI A §1 makes you deliver the receivables (Section 3.1 sensitivity); and Exhibit A as filed would be a written allocation "binding on them" (library: `irc_197_and_noncompete`) against the IRS for both parties. LOI A §5 makes the LOI "Non-binding except confidentiality and exclusivity (45 days)" — non-binding terms, but the exclusivity may already bind you alone (Section 10.1).

172: 
173: ### 6.1 The counter (full justification and filing mechanics in `form_8594_counter.md`)

176: |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
177: | III | Receivables | $200,000 | $200,000 | $200,000 (assumed) | $0 | — |
178: | IV | Inventory | $150,000 | $140,000 | $140,000 | $0 | — |
179: | V | Equipment & vehicles | $900,000 | $650,000 | $240,000 | $410,000 | Ordinary in full |
180: | VI | Non-compete | $400,000 | $100,000 | $0 | $100,000 | Ordinary |
181: | VII | Goodwill (residual) | $1,450,000 | $2,010,000 | $0 | $2,010,000 | LTCG |
182: | | **Total** | $3,100,000 | **$3,100,000** | | $2,520,000 | $510,000 ord / $2,010,000 cap |

184: Tax: 37% × $510,000 = $188,700; 20% × $2,010,000 = $402,000; shareholder $590,700; entity §1374 $237,300 (unchanged — Section 4.3); total $828,000; **net $2,272,000**. **Gain: $2,272,000 − $2,176,800 = $95,200.**
185: 
186: The arithmetic identity: every dollar moved from Class IV/V/VI into the Class VII residual moves from 37% to 20% — **17 points** — and triggers no extra §1374 because both caps are already fully absorbed:

188: | Fix | Dollars | Value (17%) |
189: |---|---:|---:|
190: | Equipment $900,000 → $650,000 (your own register's FMV) | $250,000 | $42,500 |
191: | Covenant $400,000 → $100,000 (economic-reality rule, Section 3.4) | $300,000 | $51,000 |
192: | Inventory $150,000 → $140,000 (CPA carrying value) | $10,000 | $1,700 |
193: | **Total** | | **$95,200** |

195: ### 6.2 Why covenant $100,000 and not $0
196: 
197: $0 is the economically honest number against the appraisal and the Hensley datapoint, and it is worth the most: covenant at $0 yields ordinary $410,000, capital $2,110,000, tax $573,700 + $237,300 = $811,000, **net $2,289,000** (+$112,200 vs. drafted). But a signed exhibit that pays you **nothing** for a 5-year covenant you refuse to walk away from invites exactly the re-characterization the library warns about: the written allocation is binding absent "strong proof" and the IRS may challenge an allocation that does not reflect economic reality (`irc_197_and_noncompete`). A deal with a 5-year covenant and literally zero allocated to it is the classic fact pattern for the IRS to pull dollars out of goodwill into ordinary income — with interest — on an allocation you signed. **Counter at $100,000 (judgement, labelled), concede toward $0 only in exchange for price, and never below a token real number.** Tier map (same equipment and inventory lines throughout):

199: | Covenant | Ordinary | Capital | Total tax | Net |
200: |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
201: | $0 | $410,000 | $2,110,000 | $811,000 | $2,289,000 |
202: | $100,000 | $510,000 | $2,010,000 | $828,000 | $2,272,000 |
203: | $400,000 (drafted) | $1,070,000 | $1,450,000 | $923,200 | $2,176,800 |
204: 
205: Each $100,000 of covenant costs you $17,000. That is the price of the risk shield — say so out loud when you negotiate it.
206: 
207: ### 6.3 What Lone Star's concessions are actually worth to them (know your trading currency)
208: 
209: Your allocation fixes shift roughly $550,000–$650,000 of buyer amortization between classes but change **nothing** in what Lone Star pays — its cost is only the *timing* of its own deductions (equipment depreciates faster than 15-year §197/goodwill amortization). At a 21% corporate rate the gross shield on the $250,000 equipment reduction is $52,500, and its present-value timing edge is only on the order of $13,000–$15,000 (illustrative: 7-year recovery vs. 15-year, half-year convention, 8–12% discount; **MACRS schedules and PV math are not in the library — directional estimate only**). So: fixing Exhibit A to your own documented FMV costs Lone Star pocket change; you should not "pay" for it with price. The $400,000→$100,000 covenant cut genuinely *helps* Lone Star's optics too (it is their exhibit that violates the FMV rule they want you to sign). The trade to propose: **their exhibit corrected, your signature this week, price unchanged** — and if they insist on keeping Exhibit A as drafted, the fallback is price: $95,200 ÷ 0.80 = **+$119,000** (each extra dollar nets 80 cents — Section 4.3) restores your $2,272,000 at $3,219,000.
210: 
211: ### 6.4 Parity prices — what Lone Star must pay to beat Hensley (all net-80¢, §1374 flat)
212: 
213: Measured against Hensley's clean stock net of $2,364,000 (before note interest; add $70,875 of price per $56,700 of interest you value):
214: 
215: | Lone Star structure | Net at $3,100,000 | Price needed to match $2,364,000 |
216: |---|---:|---:|
217: | Exhibit A as drafted | $2,176,800 | $3,334,000 (+$234,000) |
218: | Counter allocation | $2,272,000 | $3,215,000 (+$115,000) |

1: # Memorandum — Brightline Cabinetry LLC: Lone Star asset LOI vs. Hensley stock LOI
2: 
3: **To:** Ray Brightline
4: **From:** Tax comparison engagement
5: **Date:** October 26, 2026
6: **Re:** Lone Star Millwork Holdings LLC ($3,100,000 asset purchase LOI, March 30, 2026) vs. Hensley Family Partners LP ($2,850,000 membership-interest LOI, April 2, 2026) — after-tax comparison, Form 8594 allocation counter, and what your "$2.5M net" estimate missed.
7: 
8: **Sources.** Facts come only from your file: the two LOIs, the prior CPA's tax-history memo, the fixed-asset register, and your email. Law comes only from the reference library in this workspace (`library/INDEX.md` — seven items). Anything outside that library is labelled as an estimate, an inference, or unverified, and is not cited. Numbers to be confirmed are in `QUESTIONS.md`; none of them changes the ranking.
9: 
10: ---
11: 
12: ## 1. Bottom line
13: 
14: | | Lone Star as drafted | Lone Star with our counter allocation | Hensley stock sale |
15: |---|---:|---:|---:|
16: | Price / consideration | $3,100,000 | $3,100,000 | $2,850,000 |
17: | Ordinary income (37%) | $1,070,000 | $510,000 | $0 |
18: | Long-term capital gain (20%) | $1,450,000 | $2,010,000 | $2,430,000 |
19: | Shareholder-level tax | $685,900 | $590,700 | $486,000 |
20: | Entity-level §1374 tax (21%) | $237,300 | $237,300 | $0 |
21: | **Total tax** | **$923,200** | **$828,000** | **$486,000** |
22: | **Net after tax** | **$2,176,800** | **$2,272,000** | **$2,364,000** |
23: 
24: (Hensley's figure excludes the note's interest; the interest adds $56,700 after tax — Section 7.2. All figures are nominal and undiscounted; definitions in Section 1.2.)
25: 
26: **Hensley pays $250,000 less and leaves you $187,200 more than Lone Star as drafted — even before its note pays you interest.** Lone Star's own allocation is what makes its bigger price smaller: the $400,000 you would book to the non-compete is ordinary at 37%, and its $900,000 equipment line exceeds documented fair value, so all $660,000 of equipment gain is §1245 recapture at 37%. Fixing the allocation at the same $3,100,000 is worth $95,200 to you. Even then, Hensley still leads the repaired Lone Star deal by $92,000 — Hensley's structure avoids both the ordinary-income trap and the $237,300 entity-level tax outright.
27: 
28: ### 1.1 The three things that drive the entire result
29: 
30: 1. **Your S corporation is still inside the five-year built-in-gains recognition period.** The S election is effective January 1, 2023 (CPA memo), and the library states the recognition period is the "5-year period beginning with the first day of the first taxable year for which the corporation was an S corporation" (library: `irc_1374`). A 2026 closing is inside it. An asset sale by an S corporation in the period triggers a **corporate-level tax of $237,300** that a stock sale does not trigger at all — and you cannot reduce it by moving money between asset classes, because the law limits recognized built-in gain to each asset's built-in gain at the start of the period (Section 4).
31: 2. **Lone Star's allocation manufactures ordinary income.** Under the library, covenant payments to a seller are ordinary income and recapture is ordinary (library: `irc_197_and_noncompete`, `irc_1245`, `stock_vs_asset_overview`). As drafted, $1,070,000 — 35% of the price — is taxed at 37% instead of 20%.
32: 3. **Almost none of the price is sheltered by basis.** Your stock basis is $420,000 (CPA memo, as of 12/31/2025) and the company's aggregate inside asset basis is $580,000 (register equipment $240,000 + CPA-memo inventory $140,000 + receivables $200,000 if the receivables carry full basis — Section 3.1), against prices of $2.85M and $3.1M. And inside basis exceeds your outside basis by $160,000, which an asset sale largely wastes (Section 8.4).
33: 
34: ### 1.2 What "net after tax" means here (and what it does not)
35: 
36: - Headline net = consideration minus (shareholder-level tax + entity-level §1374 tax), **nominal and undiscounted**.
37: - Hensley's note interest ($90,000 total, $56,700 after tax at 37%) is a return *on* the note, not on the deal; it is reported separately, not in the headline. Including it, Hensley's nominal net is $2,420,700.
38: - Excluded because the file gives no amounts: company liabilities (Lone Star's LOI §1 assumes only scheduled trade payables; Hensley assumes everything, known and unknown), the $100,000 Hensley escrow, and the 10% indemnity cap. These are risk items, not taxes — Sections 7.4 and 10.
39: - Your stock basis is assumed unchanged from 12/31/2025 to the closing date; the file gives no 2026 activity (QUESTIONS.md).
40: 
41: ### 1.3 Recommendation (detail in Section 10)
42: 
43: Pursue Hensley at $2,850,000 — but use a corrected Lone Star allocation (Section 6) both to force Lone Star to pay for its defective exhibit and to make Hensley compete. Do not sign the Lone Star LOI as drafted. Do not give Hensley §338(h)(10)/§336(e) consent for free — a deemed asset sale at their price costs you $276,700–$387,200 (Section 7.5). And do not let the non-compete or consulting work become uncompensated ordinary income dressed up as part of the price.
44: 
45: ---
46: 
47: ## 2. Rates and the arithmetic conventions
48: 
49: All rates from the library (`capital_gain_rates.md`): ordinary income **37%**; long-term capital gain **20%**; the §1374 corporate tax is at the highest corporate rate, **21%** (library: `irc_1374` (b)(1)). **No Texas individual income tax** — the library states "Texas has no individual income tax" (`capital_gain_rates`); the CPA memo agrees. The CPA memo also notes "franchise tax applies to the entity" — the library contains no franchise-tax authority, so it is **not modeled** and is an open item (Section 11).
50: 
51: **The 3.8% net investment income tax is assumed not to apply.** The library's sentence is: "the 3.8% net investment income tax does **not** apply to gain from an active trade or business in which the taxpayer materially participates" (`capital_gain_rates`). That is conditioned on material participation; you have run this company since 2012, so we apply it as an assumption about your facts, not as a legal conclusion about your return. If it were held to apply, add 3.8% to the capital-gain rate — roughly $92,340 on the Hensley gain; it is in QUESTIONS.md.
52: 
53: Gain = amount realized minus adjusted basis; basis recovery is not taxed but reduces what is. That is the standard method; the library does not spell the formula out, so it is labelled as such wherever it does work (Sections 3, 8).
54: 
55: ---
56: 
57: ## 3. Character of each gain component, with authority
58: 
59: ### 3.1 Receivables — $200,000; zero gain assumed, but the basis is an assumption
60: 
61: The CPA memo shows "receivables $200,000.00 (no reserve)." That is a book carrying value; **the file nowhere states their tax basis, and it nowhere states the company's method of accounting** (the fixed-asset register has no receivables line). Lone Star's LOI §1 lists receivables among the assets bought, and Exhibit A allocates the full $200,000 to Class III (the library's §1060 class list: "III mark-to-market assets and receivables").
62: 
63: **Base case (assumption, labelled):** basis = face = $200,000, so zero gain at either price.
64: **Sensitivity (labelled):** if the company keeps its books on the cash method, billed-but-uncollected receivables typically carry no tax basis, and the $200,000 would be **ordinary income when collected or on sale** — worth $200,000 × 37% = **$74,000** of extra tax. That would cut the counter allocation's net to $2,198,000 and widen Hensley's lead to $166,000. The accounting method is question 1 of `QUESTIONS.md`; it moves dollars, not the ranking.
65: 
66: ### 3.2 Inventory — $150,000 as drafted; $10,000 of ordinary margin
67: 
68: CPA memo: "Inventory (materials) carrying value $140,000.00." Exhibit A allocates $150,000 (Class IV, the library's inventory class). The $10,000 excess over the $140,000 carrying value is ordinary income under the standard method (inventory is not a capital asset; also §1060's residual method itself puts inventory in its own class, and the library's §453 text confirms inventory sales are excluded from installment treatment, consistent with their ordinary character). $10,000 × 37% = $3,700 as drafted; we counter inventory at $140,000 (Section 6).
69: 
70: ### 3.3 Equipment and vehicles — $900,000 as drafted vs. $650,000 documented FMV; all-ordinary under §1245
71: 
72: Register totals: cost $1,100,000, accumulated depreciation $860,000, adjusted basis **$240,000**, FMV estimate **$650,000**.
73: 
74: Library rule (`irc_1245`): on disposition of §1245 property, "the amount by which the lower of (A) the recomputed basis of the property, or (B) the amount realized, exceeds the adjusted basis of such property **shall be treated as ordinary income**," where "Recomputed basis = adjusted basis plus depreciation allowed or allowable."
75: 
76: - Recomputed basis = $240,000 + $860,000 = **$1,100,000**.
77: - As drafted: amount realized $900,000. Lower of (A) $1,100,000 and (B) $900,000 is $900,000. Ordinary income = $900,000 − $240,000 = **$660,000 — the entire gain, none of it capital gain.**
78: - At documented FMV $650,000: lower of $1,100,000 and $650,000 is $650,000; ordinary income = $650,000 − $240,000 = **$410,000**, saving ($660,000 − $410,000) × 17 points = **$42,500** (Section 6).
79: - Note the ceiling: every allocated dollar above $1,100,000 would have escaped recapture as capital gain. Lone Star chose $900,000 — below the ceiling, above your own FMV evidence, which maximizes ordinary income. That is not accidental and it is not "standard."
80: 
81: ### 3.4 The non-compete — $400,000 as drafted; ordinary income, and attackable as overstated
82: 
83: Library (`irc_197_and_noncompete`): "A covenant not to compete entered into in connection with the acquisition of a trade or business is a section 197 intangible amortizable by the buyer over 15 years. **To the seller, payments for a covenant not to compete are ordinary income** (compensation for refraining from competing), not capital gain." So the drafted $400,000 (Class VI, which the library's §1060 list defines as "section 197 intangibles other than goodwill (including covenants not to compete)") is **$400,000 × 37% = $148,000** of tax instead of $80,000 — a $68,000 penalty at the drafted size.
84: 
85: The same library entry gives the attack: "Allocation between a covenant and goodwill must reflect economic reality; the parties' written allocation is binding on them (§1060(a); *Danielson* rule) absent strong proof, and the IRS may challenge it" (citing Rev. Rul. 69-643; *Muskat v. United States*, 554 F.3d 183 (1st Cir. 2009)). Three facts in your own file are the "strong proof" direction:
86: 
87: - The 2023 conversion appraisal values exactly two assets — goodwill/trade name $900,000 and equipment $610,000 — **no covenant value at all** (CPA memo table).
88: - Hensley's LOI §4 shows a market data point: "No non-compete payment; Seller signs a customary 3-year non-compete as part of the purchase agreement at no separate consideration." A second buyer is getting a 3-year covenant for nothing.
89: - Lone Star's clause §4 bundles the covenant with a **consulting** obligation ("5-year non-competition and consulting agreement; $400,000.00 of the price is allocated to it") — so the $400,000 is doing double duty and is very likely mis-sized in both directions.
90: 
91: Two-edged discipline follows: we counter the covenant **down** to $100,000 but not to $0 (Section 6.2), and **any consulting you actually perform is separately priced outside the purchase price** — consulting fees are compensation for services, an inference the library does not expressly state, but the point is protective either way: if the IRS re-characterized part of the covenant as services income you would get no capital treatment, and if you work for a year for nothing inside the price you have financed the deal twice.
92: 
93: ### 3.5 Goodwill and the residual — Class VII, zero basis
94: 
95: Library §1060 rule: consideration is allocated among seven classes "in order" — I cash; II actively traded personal property; III mark-to-market assets and receivables; IV inventory; V all other assets (equipment, real property); VI §197 intangibles other than goodwill (including covenants); VII goodwill and going concern value — and "**Each class is allocated up to fair market value before moving to the next.**" Goodwill is the residual: everything the buyer pays above the earlier classes' FMV lands in Class VII.
96: 
97: Goodwill/trade-name adjusted basis at 1/1/2023 was **$0** (CPA memo appraisal table), so Class VII gain is capital gain in full at 20% (capital character of goodwill: library's asset-sale description assigns recapture and covenants to ordinary, leaving the balance as gain under the allocation; `stock_vs_asset_overview`). Each dollar moved out of over-filled ordinary classes into Class VII saves 17 points (37 − 20 cents).
98: 
99: ### 3.6 Exhibit A, as drafted, cannot be filed — it violates the residual method twice
100: 
101: The library's rule caps each class at fair market value: "Each class is allocated up to fair market value before moving to the next" (`irc_1060_form_8594.md`).
102: 
103: 1. **Class V is filled above FMV.** Exhibit A allocates $900,000 to equipment & vehicles; your own register says $650,000. The excess $250,000 is exactly the dollars Lone Star moved out of the goodwill residual to manufacture §1245 ordinary income.
104: 2. **Class I is missing.** Exhibit A totals $3,100,000 across Classes III–VII only. There is no Class I line for cash in the company at closing. If the company holds any cash (QUESTIONS.md), Exhibit A is short by that amount and cannot balance a Form 8594 for a $3.1M purchase of assets plus whatever cash transfers.
105: 3. Also note: Exhibit A's Class VII goodwill is $1,450,000, while the 2023 appraisal valued goodwill/trade name at $900,000. Growth to 2026 is plausible (this is the residual, so it absorbs whatever remains), but do not present the appraisal as "supporting" Exhibit A — it predates it and values goodwill $550,000 lower.
106: 
107: ---
108: 
109: ## 4. The §1374 built-in gains tax: $237,300 in every asset-sale scenario, and why you cannot allocate your way out of it
110: 
111: ### 4.1 You are inside the recognition period
112: 
113: Library (`irc_1374`): "(a) If for any taxable year beginning in the **recognition period** an S corporation has a net recognized built-in gain, there is imposed a tax… (b)(1) The tax is the highest corporate rate (**21%**) on the net recognized built-in gain. (d)(7) The recognition period is the **5-year period beginning with the first day of the first taxable year for which the corporation was an S corporation.**"
114: 
115: The CPA memo: "Elected S corporation status effective January 1, 2023 (Form 2553 accepted)." Recognition period = **January 1, 2023 through December 31, 2027**. Any 2026 or 2027 closing is inside it.
116:
